So Linux, in a nutshell, is nothing but the kernel of the operating system. It is what talks to all your hardware, the CPU, the keyboard and mouse, your monitor, it does all the heavy lifting, but that is ALL is does. Linux itself has no applications, that's what the distributions(henceforth known as "distro") are for. So they grab a kernel, build the necessary software that works with the kernel, and ship it out as a distribution.

The distributions themselves are widely varied. There are many general use and specialty distros. Linux runs many things you might not think about, all of my routers and switches at home run Linux. It's under the covers of a pretty GUI, but its just Linux underneath. So back to the distros, there are several larger competing package management systems, some better than others, but all pretty much the same in that they perform the same functions. Most will download the necessary packages to install any particular package, including any prerequisites that package may need.

The competing package managers are the biggest difference in the major distributions. Redhat/Fedora/SuSE and many off-shoots use the "rpm" or "RedHat Package Manager". Debian/Ubuntu and any off-shoots use "apt". ArchLinux and any offshots use "pacman". I woudn't worry about the difference for now, once you choose a distro, then you can familiarize yourself with the package manager. At this point, they are all pretty polished and easy to use. Myself, I prefer debian based packing(apt), but also use rpm on a regular basis both at home and at work.

Choosing a distro, my favorites are Ubuntu and Debian. I am currently running 15.04(Vivid Vervet) available here. Another good Debian/Ubuntu based distro is "Mint", available here. So I would suggest one of those, at least to get started.

As for what makes it special, for a basic OS user, just running the occasional spreadsheet and a browser, the best takeaway is that its free(cost) and incredibly stable. It just works, all the time. I have a server at work with over 900 days of uptime. For a more power user, the power lies in what you can do in Linux. You can customize almost EVERYTHING in Linux. You can completely change the look and feel at anytime. You can run virtual machines, and almost everything is free, many in cost, and most in that they are open source. You can actually go out and see the code that runs the applications. Im not a programmer, for the most part, but have provided code to a number of open source projects to fix either annoyances or an oversight in the functionality of the program.

With Linux, you can go as deep as you want, or just swim on top. That's the beauty of Linux, its up to YOU what YOU want. And it fosters a great community to help you out.

Ubuntu has an online tour you can give a try. It explains some of the features and show you how the OS looks.

http://tour.ubuntu.com/en/

I'll preface this by saying that I know it'll sound offensive, and course, but that's not my intent. Let's work through your post backwards, to kelp clear things up:

Before that, though could someone please tell me what Linux is in a nutshell? I know it's an operating system

This actually isn't correct. Linux is a kernel, meaning it doesn't consist of drivers, system files, or any of the desktop interfaces you're used to. It's just the code that let's all of that communicate with your computer's hardware. It's kind of like the middle-management of your computer, where the software and drivers tell the hardware what to do, and the hardware does all the manual labor, and the kernel is the translator and mailman at the same time.

Think about booting into a Terminal screen, with only a command prompt... It's actually less than that. You need to add a bootloader to be able to boot into it, and so on and so forth.

BSD is an operating system, but Linux is just a kernel.

I just want the "official" verson of Linux, without having to jump through "distros" and "GNUs" and "source codes."

You can grab the Linux kernel here, but at this point, it probably won't be useful to you... It's more for people who want to play with the source code, and make their system completely custom.

As I said before, the kernel itself is pretty useless without all of the other "overhead" stuff to make it work.

there are a million different versions

These are the distros you were talking about. These are designed to add a graphical interface for you to use. They also add a way to manage programs, called a package manager, like the appstore on your phone.

Some are easier to use, and some require quite a bit of knowledge to use correctly... Which is why most people here suggest Mint or ElementaryOS. These are both easy enough to use for beginners, and they are "genuine Linux" distros, so it'll grow with you. The more you learn, the more you'll be able to do.
Just about every distro is based on Debian. You do not want Debian. Sit down, do your research, and make an educated decision.

Linux is just a tool. A part of a toolset (Linux distribution). Like a car engine being part of car. You are looking for a car, and you're asking for "official version of a car engine" without having to jump through "different car brands", "Toyotas", "hybrids", "SUVs" etc.
